title: collaborate / corroborate / elaborate
core: Three long Latin verbs that rhyme, share the -orate ending, and all describe doing something *to* a piece of work or a claim — building it with someone, propping it up, or filling it out. Two of them genuinely descend from *labor* (work); the middle one comes from *robur* (strength) and only sounds like a sibling. Nothing about their meanings actually overlaps once you stop looking at the letters, which is exactly why the exam pairs them.

words.nuance: **Collaborate** is the only one that requires a *second person* — you cannot collaborate alone. It is also the only one with a treason sense: under occupation the word flips from praise to accusation, and *collaborator* carries the stain hardest. If war, occupation, or resistance sits anywhere nearby, the word is an indictment.

**Corroborate** needs a *prior claim*, not a partner — it arrives second, adding independent evidence to something already asserted. It only strengthens; it never proves the case alone, and it never counts if it comes from the source that made the claim. Its home is the courtroom, the lab, the newsroom — the one word here that sounds stiff in casual speech.

**Elaborate** needs neither a partner nor a claim to lean on — it is about *detail and effort*, and it is the only one that also works as an adjective. As a verb it means to say more about your own point; as an adjective it admires the labour visible in a thing, then sours the instant that labour looks disproportionate (*elaborate hoax*, *elaborate excuse*).

exam_note: The classic trap is a sentence about a second witness or a lab result offering "collaborate" — testimony *corroborates*; only people collaborate.
